title: A Stormy Thanksgiving Across America
summary:
Thanksgiving looked different this year for millions of Americans. Storms swept across the country on Thursday, bringing floods, strong winds, and power outages that changed holiday plans from coast to coast.

By Thursday evening, more than 900,000 customers in at least eight states had lost power. On the East Coast, two storm systems stretched from Maine to Florida. On the West Coast, strong winds battered the shore from Oregon to California.

The wind hit hard. In Ocean City, Maryland, gusts of up to 65 miles per hour ripped the roof off a building. Near Washington, D.C., similar gusts tossed a tree into a house where people were inside. Officials said no one was hurt.

Floodwater swamped coastal towns, nearly covering downtown Stone Harbor, New Jersey. New Jersey and New York both declared states of emergency. Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci of MyRadar.com warned that power outages could keep rising. He explained that a fast river of wind high above the ground, moving at about 80 miles per hour, was feeding the storms below.

Some places got a white Thanksgiving instead, including St. Louis and western Tennessee. Travelers had a rough day too. By late afternoon, FlightAware counted more than 1,900 flight delays and over 400 cancellations.

Out west, huge tides called king tides pounded the coast. In Pacifica, California, a pier partly collapsed, and the town's seawall now faces big repairs. Cappucci said this year's super El Nino, a climate event, is making things worse, pushing water levels up by three feet or more in some places.

Even the parades felt it. The 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed until Saturday, and Philadelphia moved its parade indoors. The storm was expected to keep affecting parts of the country through Friday.
why_it_matters: Storms like these show how quickly severe weather can shut down power, travel, and public events for millions of people at once, and why warnings and emergency plans matter before a holiday when so many people are on the move.

background_read: Thanksgiving is a major holiday in the United States, when families gather for a big meal and many people travel long distances to be together, so bad weather on that day can disrupt plans for millions of people at once.
Big storms form when warm and cold air meet and strong winds high in the sky feed clouds and rain below, and they can bring floods, power cuts, and dangerous gusts all at the same time.
Along the coast, the danger grows when high tides and storm winds push ocean water onto land, and walls built to hold back the sea can be damaged.
El Nino is a natural warming of part of the Pacific Ocean that can shift weather patterns around the world, sometimes making storms and high water worse.
